A small request within royal control

The four accept new names, a foreign education, and royal service. Verse 8 shows where Daniel draws his line: the king’s table. He decides in his heart, and then he asks. He does not defy the official. His proposal protects that official too (verses 10–13). The test is short, and its result can be checked. The chapter says three times that “God gave” (verses 2, 9, 17).
The threatened servants and the fragile statue

The statue’s metals fall in value from the head to the feet. It ends in iron mixed with brittle clay. Verse 34 says the stone was cut “without hands.” No human power made it. Verse 44 says this kingdom will not pass to another people. That sets it apart from every kingdom in the statue. Daniel’s answer saves the other wise men, and he takes no credit (verses 24, 30).
Refusal does not depend on rescue

The king asks in verse 15 what god could rescue them. Their reply has two parts. Verse 17 says their God is able. Verse 18 begins, “But if not.” They do not claim to know what will happen. Their refusal does not depend on being saved. Verse 25 notes that the men walk “loose,” so the fire burned only their ropes.
The ruler must learn what his power serves

The tree in the dream gave food and shade to all (verse 12). A king’s greatness was meant to shelter others. Daniel’s advice in verse 27 is specific. The king should do what is right and show mercy to the poor. Verse 29 shows he had twelve months to act. Verse 30 gives his boast: “I have built” and “my power.” The story is told in the voice of the king who learned it.
Stolen vessels expose a ruler's blindness

Daniel refuses the rewards before he reads a word (verse 17). His message is not for sale. Verse 22 says the king knew what happened to Nebuchadnezzar. Knowing the story did not change him. Verse 23 states the charge in two parts. He used holy cups to praise gods that cannot see or hear. He did not honor the God who holds his breath.
Ordinary prayer becomes a legal trap

Daniel’s rivals build their trap from his known habit (verse 5). Verse 10 says he prayed “as he did before.” He does not hide, and he does not make a display. He simply continues. The law also traps the king who signed it. Verses 14–15 show the most powerful man in the land unable to help. He can only hope that Daniel’s God will (verse 16).
The court limits the beasts' power

The kingdoms in this vision appear as animals. The one who finally rules appears as a human figure. Verse 14 says rule “was given” to him; he does not seize it. Verses 9–10 make the turning point a court, not a battle. Verses 18 and 27 give the same kingdom to God’s holy people. Verse 28 says Daniel remained troubled. Jesus draws on this scene in Mark 14:62.
Power attacks worship and exhausts the witness

Gabriel comes close, and Daniel falls on his face in fear (verse 17). The angel then names the kingdoms outright (verses 20–21). That is rare in visions of this kind. Even so, verse 27 says Daniel was ill and did not understand. Named explanations do not remove the weight of what he saw. Verse 25 says the last king is broken “without hand.” The stone of 2:34 was described the same way.
Confession asks for mercy beyond earned reward

Verse 2 shows the prayer beginning from a text, the scroll of Jeremiah. The story has shown Daniel as faithful, yet he says “we” throughout. Verse 18 states his ground plainly. He does not ask because the people deserve it. He asks because God’s mercies are great. Verse 19 adds that the city and people carry God’s name. Readers have understood the seventy weeks of verses 24–27 in very different ways.
The unseen conflict meets a weakened body

Daniel mourned and fasted for three full weeks (verses 2–3). Verse 12 says his words were heard on the first day. Verse 13 explains the delay as a conflict he could not see. It lasted twenty-one days, the same three weeks. The wait is not blamed on the one who prayed. The messenger touches him three times (verses 10, 16, 18). Each touch restores a little more of his strength.
Broken alliances do not stop faithful teaching

Verses 32–33 describe faithful people under a violent ruler. They know their God, stand firm, and teach others. Verse 33 admits that they fall by sword, fire, and prison. Verse 35 gives that suffering a purpose and a limit. It refines them, and it lasts only until the appointed time. Their fall is not counted as failure. The alliances earlier in the chapter all collapse (verses 6 and 17).
Hope includes waiting without full understanding

Verse 2 gives the clearest statement of resurrection in the Old Testament. Verse 3 names those who will shine. They are the wise who turn many to righteousness. These are the teachers of 11:33, some of whom were killed. In verse 8 Daniel says he does not understand and asks more. Verse 9 does not explain. Verse 13 gives him a promise for himself: rest, and a place at the end.
